title: The Borrowed Letter
premise: When the town of Marrow's End exhumes its founder, Aldous Wren, for a ceremonial reburial, the coffin holds only stones and a single typewritten letter signed with a name no one recognizes. Retired detective Tamsin Kavanagh, whose bookshop is weeks from closing, is dragged back into investigative work when the letter's phrasing echoes an unsolved disappearance from thirty years ago—one Tamsin was quietly forced off. Following the letter through the town's founding families, Tamsin discovers that Aldous Wren never existed as the man buried; he was an identity stolen, worn by someone who built an empire on a borrowed name and a buried body. The killer is the town's current matriarch, who helped steal the identity as a young woman and has been eliminating witnesses as the exhumation loomed; the final letter was her own confession, planted to be read only after her death—but she isn't dead yet, and Tamsin must prove a murder whose victim has no name.
about_author: Noor Ravensworth is a former small-town archivist who spent years cataloguing the paper trails people leave behind, an obsession that now fuels her fiction. She writes mysteries about quiet places where old secrets compound like interest, and lives somewhere with unreliable weather and excellent secondhand bookshops.

chapters.title: The Exhumation
chapters.summary: Third-person limited from Tamsin's POV. Marrow's End opens its founder's grave for a centennial reburial, and the crowd falls silent at the empty coffin and the stones. Tamsin, watching from the back of his failing bookshop, feels the old detective reflex stir against his will. Emotional beat: dread disguised as curiosity—the past has knocked on his door.

chapters.title: Stones and Paper
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The coroner dismisses it as a prank, but Tamsin recognizes the typewriter font of the letter left in the coffin—it matches a case file from thirty years ago that he was ordered to abandon. He digs out his old notes at night, alone in the shop. Emotional beat: reluctant reawakening; the shop's debts press on him, making the detective's return feel like both failure and rescue.

chapters.title: The Wren Archives
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He visits the Wren estate's archive, where matriarch Vivian Wren receives him with velvet hostility and grants access only to curated records. He finds a photograph of young Aldous whose face doesn't match later portraits. Emotional beat: unease sharpening into certainty that the town's origin story is a forgery—and that Vivian knows he's looking.

chapters.title: A Face That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Alternating Tamsin's POV with a 1994 flashback from a missing woman, Edith Marsh, the town librarian who vanished. Edith recognized Aldous Wren as a man she'd known under another name and wrote a letter she never sent. Emotional beat: the reader feels the trap closing on Edith while Tamsin, in the present, finds her unsent letter hidden in a donated book—literally on his own shelves.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibis
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He interviews the founding families' aging heirs and finds their alibis for the week Edith vanished are suspiciously identical, word for word—as if rehearsed. Someone breaks into his bookshop that night, taking nothing but the old case notes. Emotional beat: isolation and menace; the town closes ranks, and Tamsin realizes invisibility was protection he no longer has.

chapters.title: The Second Grave
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with a brief Edith flashback. Following land records, Tamsin finds an unmarked grave on the old Wren orchard. The body is exhumed quietly: Edith Marsh, and beside her remains, a man whose jaw doesn't match the famous Aldous portraits. The real Aldous Wren was murdered in 1993 and his identity worn by an impostor. Emotional beat: grim vindication curdling into fear—he now knows too much to stop.

chapters.title: What Vivian Knew
chapters.summary: Vivian Wren's POV for the first time. She recalls, without remorse, how she and the impostor—her late husband—built Marrow's End on a stolen name, and how Edith's discovery required 'tidying.' She learns the orchard grave has been found. Emotional beat: chilling intimacy with the antagonist; power as habit, corruption as housekeeping.

chapters.title: Fire and Ash
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. His bookshop is set ablaze; he escapes with the unsent Edith letter and the case notes, but his archive of thirty years burns. The fire is ruled accidental; the police chief, whose career Vivian built, won't hear otherwise. Emotional beat: lowest point—Tamsin has lost his shop, his refuge, and any illusion that the law is neutral. He decides to finish it anyway.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Letter
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, climax. At the centennial reburial ceremony, before the whole town, Tamsin reads the letter from the coffin aloud—it is Edith's, describing the impostor's true name, and it names the young woman who helped him: Vivian. Confronted before the town whose loyalty is her armor, Vivian's composure cracks when Tamsin produces the typewriter itself, preserved from the old evidence room. Emotional beat: cathartic exposure; the borrowed letter returns to its true author.

chapters.title: What Remains
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, resolution. Vivian, facing charges, reveals where Edith's own writings lie, restoring her name to the town record. The impostor's identity is published; Marrow's End must decide what to do with a history built on a lie. Tamsin, using insurance and a town ashamed enough to be generous, reopens the bookshop with a shelf dedicated to Edith Marsh. Emotional beat: quiet repair—identity restored to the dead, and Tamsin choosing to be visible at last.
